title: The open-plan experiment
text: The open-plan office {{1}} from post-war rationalism: walls cost money, and the factory floor suggested a model for {{2}} work. The promises were collaboration, flexibility and equality — no corner offices, nobody hidden away. The research has been {{3}}. Workers in open plans take more sick days, report more interruptions, and — in the {{4}} finding — talk less about work than colleagues behind walls, because every conversation {{5}} an audience. Face-to-face interaction does rise, but much of it is {{6}}: a glance, a greeting, a deflected question. The market has been adjusting {{7}}: screens, booths and bookable glass rooms have crept back in, and hybrid working has turned the office itself into a destination for exactly the collaborative days the open plan was built for. The deeper lesson survives every redesign: attention is the scarcest {{8}} in a workplace, and any layout that spends it casually will pay for it in kind.

gaps.explanation: 'the open-plan office emerged from post-war rationalism' — arose out of it; engulf = swallow up.
'a model for organising work' — arranging how it is done; ostracise = exclude from a group.
'the research has been brutal' — merciless to the idea; brusque = abrupt in manner, brazen = shameless.
'the ironic finding' — the opposite of what openness promised; iconic = famous as a symbol, irksome = irritating.
'every conversation attracts an audience' — draws listeners; avert = turn away, allot = distribute.
'much of it is trivial: a glance, a greeting' — insignificant; tribal = relating to tribes, turbulent = stormy.
'the market has been adjusting accordingly' — in line with the findings; allegedly = as is claimed without proof.
'attention is the scarcest resource' — the thing in shortest supply; restraint = holding back, residue = a remnant.
